reflection_text.2:
The deliberation is on vicarious liability of Evergreen Grass Care Ltd for Mark and Lincoln, and personal liability of the employees, with the neighbours’ role.

Mark / pool loss
* Unanimous that Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the pool cover/pool removal/clean-up loss.
* Mark was cutting grass on employer’s riding mower on the job site. Distraction by neighbour’s dog, intricate movements, reaching down from a moving mower to pick up a stick and falling, with automatic-drive mower then entering the pool, is treated as negligent operation of the mower in the course/manner of performing the authorised work.
* The deviation is not a true frolic and detour; the instrumentality, time, place and work remain those of the employer. The short fence/dog of Bruce’s neighbours is background; no duty/breach/causation to Bruce and no joint tortfeasorship. Options A and B that implicate neighbours or make Mark and Lincoln jointly liable for each other’s loss are rejected.

Lincoln / Ferrari scratches
* Core disagreement is whether Evergreen is vicariously liable for Lincoln’s blower use.
* E camp: Lincoln was raking/blowing leaves with employer’s blower on the work site. Going over the lawn area next to the Ferrari “as he normally would” is an act incidental to the authorised leaf-clearing task. Propelling small rocks and causing barely noticeable scratches is a foreseeable incident/risk of using a blower in proximity to property. Personal dislike for Bruce and admiring the car is motive evidence but does not sever the sufficiently close connection; negligence in the mode of performing the work remains course of employment. De minimis damage goes to quantum, not liability. Hence Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the Ferrari loss, separate from Mark’s loss.
* C camp: the facts point to personal animus – Lincoln despises Bruce, Bruce is absent, rocks are immediately adjacent to the car – so the wrong is intentional / malicious/reckless and motivated by personal spite, not the discharge of the employer’s business. Under that view vicarious liability does not attach, Lincoln remains personally liable only. Minimal damage is not the reason for no liability; the absence of close connection is.

Emerging belief
* Vicarious liability attaches when the tort is committed in the course of employment with sufficiently close connection. Mark clearly satisfies it.
* For Lincoln, the description “went over the area with the blower as he normally would” supports a negligent mode of performing the authorised leaf-clearing work rather than a deliberate frolic. The personal dislike is insufficient on these facts to break the employment connection; the blower use is still with employer tools, on employer time/site, and the risk of debris being propelled is inherent to the work.
* Therefore the allocation is Evergreen + Mark jointly and severally for Mark’s damage, and Evergreen + Lincoln jointly and severally for Lincoln’s damage, with no neighbour liability and no cross-liability between the two employees. That is answer E.
* Unresolved tension with C colleagues about personal animus as a frolic/intentional tort bar to vicarious liability; need to keep that distinction in mind if the problem intends to treat Lincoln’s act as an intentional wrong for personal motive.

Options eliminated: A implicates neighbours; B merges the two employees’ losses; D wrongly treats de minimis damage as a defence.
reflection_text.6:
The factual matrix is two separate heads of loss on the same job site on 1 Oct 2021.

Mark / pool loss
* Consensus across colleagues: Mark was cutting grass with Evergreen’s riding mower on Bruce’s property in the course of employment. Distraction by neighbour’s dog, intricate movements, reaching down from a moving mower to pick up a stick and falling is negligent operation of employer’s equipment in the mode of performing authorised work.
* The mower’s automatic drive continuing after the fall and driving into the pool/cover is a foreseeable consequence of that negligence. The loss is therefore recoverable from Mark personally and, by respondeat superior / vicarious liability, from Evergreen. Employer and employee are jointly and severally liable for the pool-cover/removal/cleaning loss.
* No colleague sustains neighbour liability. The unusually short fence and the dog’s return of the stick are background conditions; the chain of causation is broken by Mark’s intervening negligent operation of a motorised mower. Choices A and B which implicate neighbours or make Mark and Lincoln jointly liable for each other’s loss are wrong.

Lincoln / Ferrari scratches
* Uncontroversial that Lincoln was raking/blowing leaves with employer’s blower on the property in the course of employment.
* Disagreement is on scope of employment/vicarious liability for Evergreen for the barely noticeable scratches caused by rocks blown toward Bruce’s Ferrari.
  – E camp: Use of the blower in the area adjoining the Ferrari is the very work Lincoln was engaged to do. The act was done with employer’s tools, at employer’s site, in time and place of employment. Propulsion of debris by a blower is a foreseeable work risk. Personal motive / dislike of Bruce / admiring the car does not sever the close connection; the means and occasion remain work-connected. Minimal/de minimis damage affects only quantum, not the cause of action. Hence Evergreen is vicariously liable and Evergreen + Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the car loss.
  – C camp: The facts point to a personal animus/spite, Bruce absent, Lincoln working a rock-strewn area immediately next to the car. That is an intentional/reckless wrong for wholly personal reasons, a frolic outside proper scope, so vicarious liability does not attach. Lincoln remains personally liable but Evergreen does not.
* Under Ontario close-connection test, the E view is stronger: the act complained of is blowing the leaves with the blower “as he normally would”. The act is not a departure from employment; it is negligent performance of the authorised task. Personal animus alone does not automatically remove vicarious liability where the employment provides the opportunity, time, place and instrumentality. The intentional-wrong argument is less persuasive here than for a true assault/abuse.

Current best synthesis: Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally for Mark’s pool/mower loss; Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally for Lincoln’s car scratch loss. That is choice E. Choice C’s distinction on Lincoln rests on an over-reading of motive and on a de minimis immunity that is not recognized in law. Neighbours are not liable. No cross-liability between Mark and Lincoln.

Unresolved nuance to keep: whether the degree of personal spite could be framed as an intentional tort rather than negligence, and how courts weigh opportunity vs motive in close-connection analysis. For now majority and doctrinal fit favour E.
reflection_text.5:

* Bruce’s neighbours’ short fence / dog returning stick are background facts; no duty/causation to Bruce for pool damage and no joint/several liability. This eliminates A.

Lincoln incident – split
* Lincoln was raking/blowing leaves on the employer’s site with employer’s tools = prima facie course of employment.
* Core dispute is whether personal animus – Lincoln despises Bruce, Bruce absent, Lincoln admires car, rocks next to car – removes the tort from course of employment.
  * E camp, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,3,4,6,7,9: Act described as “went over the area with the blower as he normally would”. Using blower over rocky area adjacent to Ferrari is a negligent/incidentally harmful manner of performing the leaf-clearing task. Risk of debris propelled by blower is foreseeable incident of the work. Personal motive is irrelevant / does not sever connection. Even if malicious, it remains sufficiently connected with employment. Employer is vicariously liable; Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally liable for Ferrari scratches. Minimal/barely noticeable damage goes to quantum, not liability.
  * C camp, Colleagues 15,2,5,8: Facts point to intentional/reckless wrong motivated by personal spite / personal grudge; Lincoln noted rocks immediately adjacent to car and blew them toward it while Bruce absent. Overall attribution

* Lincoln loss: majority view is Evergreen + Lincoln jointly and severally, i.e. option E: Evergreen and Mark jointly and severally for Mark’s damage; Evergreen and Lincoln jointly and severally for Lincoln’s damage.
* Option C would be correct only if personal animus defeats vicarious liability for Lincoln, which is the minority position in this round.

reflection_text.4:

E camp – Colleagues 1,3,4,6,7,9,10,11,12,13,14 – says using the blower “as he normally would” over an area next to the car is an act incidental to the authorised leaf-clearing task, done with employer’s tools at the employer’s site. Lincoln’s personal dislike of Bruce and admiration of the car is motive evidence but does not sever the close connection between the employment and the negligent use of the blower; the act remains a negligent manner of performing the work. E

Evergreen Grass Care Ltd is vicarious-ly liable for a tort committed by an employee in the course of employment and the employee remains personally liable for his own tort, so that employer and employee are jointly and severally liable for the loss flowing from that tort. The two incidents are separate heads of loss and the liability for each is confined to the tortfeasors for that incident.

Mark
Mark was on Bruce’s property operating Evergreen’s riding mower to cut grass, i.e. the very work he was hired to do. The fall, the dislocation and the subsequent autonomous movement of the mower into the pool and through the pool cover are the foreseeable consequences of Mark’s negligent operation of the mower while he was performing that authorised task – being distracted, making intricate movements and reaching down from a moving mower to pick up a stick. That is negligence in the mode of performing an authorised act, not a true frolic or detour. The mower, the time, the place and the instrumentality are all those of the employment.

Mark is therefore personally liable in negligence for the pool-cover/removal/cleaning loss and Evergreen is vicariously liable for the same loss. Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the Mark loss. The unusually short fence and the neighbour’s dog are background conditions. The neighbours owe no duty to Bruce in respect of the pool damage and Mark’s intervening negligent operation of a motorised mower is the proximate cause. Choices that make the neighbours jointly and severally liable for Mark’s loss are wrong.

Lincoln
Lincoln was on the same site raking/blowing leaves with Evergreen’s blower, the work he was engaged to do. Going over the area next to the Ferrari with the blower “as he normally would” is an act done with employer’s tools, at the employer’s site, in the time and place of employment. The propelling of small rocks from the blower and the resulting barely noticeable scratches to the Ferrari are a negligent way of performing the authorised leaf-clearing task. The risk that a blower will move debris into adjacent property is a foreseeable work risk.

Personal animus – that Lincoln despised Bruce, admired the car and Bruce was absent – goes to motive. It does not sever the close connection where the means, occasion and opportunity for the wrong are provided by the employment and the act complained of is the negligent operation of work equipment in the ordinary course of the work. The employment provides the instrumentality and the opportunity; the tort is therefore sufficiently connected to attract vicarious liability.

Lincoln remains personally liable for his own negligence and Evergreen is vicariously liable for it. Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the car scratch loss. The minimal/de minimis character of the damage affects only quantum, not the existence of a cause of action. There is no immunity for de minimis damage and no basis to treat Lincoln’s loss as outside the scope of employment.

Hence Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for the damage that resulted from Mark’s actions, and Evergreen and Lincoln are jointly and severally liable for the damage that resulted from Lincoln’s actions. Mark and Lincoln are not jointly and severally liable with each other for each other’s loss and the neighbours are not liable. That is choice E.

reflection_text.1:
The public stance is now unanimous for E in Round 2, continuing the convergence reached after Round 1.

Mark was on Bruce’s property 1 Oct 2021 cutting grass with Evergreen’s riding mower, in work time/place with employer equipment. The fall, shoulder dislocation and the mower’s automatic-drive continuation into the pool and through the pool cover flow from negligent operation of the mower while performing the authorised mowing task. Distraction by the neighbour’s dog, intricate movements and reaching down from a moving mower to retrieve a stick is negligence in the mode of performance, at most a momentary deviation, not a true frolic/detour. Instrumentality, time, place and work remain Evergreen’s; risk of loss of control of a self-propelled mower is inherent to the business. Mark is personally liable and Evergreen is vicariously liable; Evergreen and Mark are jointly and severally liable for pool cover replacement, removal and cleaning costs. The unusually short fence and dog are background only; no duty/breach/causation against Bruce’s neighbours. Neighbours are not joint tortfeasors.

Common ground on Lincoln:
Lincoln was on the same site raking/blowing leaves with Evergreen’s blower/rake in the ordinary course of the contract, in work time with employer tools at employer’s site. Use of the blower in that work area is the very act he was hired to do. Propelling debris with a blower near client property is a foreseeable incident of leaf-clearing work. Means and occasion of the wrong — employer blower, work site, work time — remain work-connected.
Personal motive evidence — Lincoln despises Bruce, admires car, Bruce absent — is acknowledged but held not to sever sufficiently close connection under Ontario respondeat superior. The tort is negligent manner of performance of an authorised duty, not an intentional wrong done wholly for a personal reason outside scope, nor a frolic.
